case_name: Babubhai Udesinh Parmar v State of Gujarat
respondent:
State of Gujarat
Supreme Court of India

24 November 2006
Appeal (Cr.) 1635 of 2005
The Judgment was delivered by: S. B. Sinha, J.
1.  The appellant herein was a labourer. He is said to have committed a series of offences involving heinous crimes. He is involved also in a case of rape and murder of a minor girl Savita. She was sister of Shankar Bhursinh (complainant). He lodged a First Information Report on 1.07.1998 inter alia stating that he with a view to earn his livelihood came with his family to Karamsad town. facts: The appellant was a labourer who committed a series of heinous crimes, including rape and murder of a minor girl Savita.
He woke up at about 2 a.m. to answer the call of nature and did not find Savita.
Searches were made for her and on the next day morning, her dead body was found lying in the surrounding field belonging to Malabhai and Kanbhai.
The blood was found to have been oozing out from her private part.
He informed the police and was arrested by the investigating officer Mr. R.G. Patel on 12.08.2002.
issues: Whether the judicial confession made by the appellant can be relied upon as a foundation for convicting him?
Whether the court can solely rely on the retracted confession and make it a foundation for convicting the accused?
petitioner_arguments: The confession was found not only to be true but having been voluntarily made.
The same could be relied upon.
The decisions of the Apex Court have often said that the court cannot solely rely on the retracted confession and make it a foundation for convicting the accused.
respondent_arguments: Ms. Hemantika Wahi, learned counsel appearing on behalf of the State, would submit that the provisions of S. 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure contains a salutary principle and only in the event the confession is found to have been voluntarily rendered, the same can be the foundation for recording a judgment of conviction.
court_reasoning: A judicial confession undoubtedly is admissible in evidence.
A judgment of conviction can also be based on a confession if it is found to be truthful, deliberate and voluntary and if clearly proved.
The voluntary nature of the confession depends upon whether there was any threat, inducement or promise and its truth is judged on the basis of the entire prosecution case.
holding: The court held that the judicial confession made by the appellant cannot be relied upon as a foundation for convicting him, as it was not voluntarily made and did not meet the requirements of S. 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
